Ophthalmology · published research

Retinopathy of prematurity

In the randomized pilot, 670 nm treatment did not improve ROP or survival compared with usual care, although treatment was feasible. Animal oxygen-induced-retinopathy models report vascular changes.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In the randomized pilot, 670 nm treatment did not improve ROP or survival compared with usual care, although treatment was feasible. Animal oxygen-induced-retinopathy models report vascular changes.

Summary of the Evidence

The category maps to oxygen-induced retinopathy and contains five publications: two human neonatal studies and three animal reports, one of which uses both mice and rats. The human reports describe separate feasibility and pilot-trial publications; possible cohort overlap is not established in the source. No independent confirmatory clinical trial is listed. Kent et al. 2019

Human and clinical evidence

The 2015 single-arm safety and feasibility study treated 21 premature neonates and reported no skin burns or other documented adverse events. A 2019 randomized pilot enrolled 86 infants. Survival was 41 of 41 in the light group and 40 of 45 in untreated controls, p=0.057. The investigators reported no improvement in ROP or survival and concluded that delivery was feasible, with dose and delivery still requiring investigation. These pilot results do not establish efficacy in preventing treatment-requiring ROP or visual impairment.

Animal evidence

Three oxygen-induced-retinopathy publications use rats or mice. They report changes in vaso-obliteration, abnormal vessel growth, and retinal neural outcomes after red-light exposure in experimental models. These findings support biological investigation but cannot be taken as proof of benefit in premature infants, whose developing retina and exposure constraints differ.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate in-vitro or ex-vivo publication was identified in the mapped ROP records.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The neonatal studies used 670 nm red light, with daily exposure initiated soon after birth and continued during the preterm period in the pilot protocol. Animal schedules and doses differ. The study record does not establish a dose that is both effective and safe for broader clinical use.

Interpretation

Clinical work establishes feasibility but not prevention of ROP. The randomized pilot did not demonstrate improved ROP or survival. Animal outcomes justify further research only; larger trials with retinal development, treatment need, and long-term vision outcomes are necessary.

Evidence strength in source summaryRetinopathy of prematurity: No benefit shown in the pilot trial Feasibility and animal outcomes: Preliminary
Publications and records5 mapped publications: 2 human neonatal studies, including 1 single-arm safety and feasibility report with 21 infants and 1 randomized pilot with 86 infants, plus 3 animal publications involving rats or mice.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The mapping contains two human studies and three animal publications, including one mouse-and-rat report. A small feasibility study found no documented skin burns, while the randomized pilot did not improve ROP or survival. Animal vascular findings do not establish benefit in premature infants.

Publication and study types

  • Animal-model labels overlap within one paper.
  • The two human reports are distinct publications; cohort overlap is not reported.
